author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Promise That Outlives the Will Behind It
subtitle: A promise regularly keeps binding after the feeling, the belief or the friendship that produced it has gone, and the theory that locates its force in an act of will cannot explain why.
abstract: The common explanation for why a promise binds is that the promisor's own will creates the obligation: to promise is to perform a small act of self-binding legislation. That explanation fails the case it should handle best, a promise whose motivating feeling has evaporated but that still binds. David Hume's dissection of the "act of mind" behind promising, and the reliance-based accounts that followed him, locate the obligation's real support outside the promisor's state of mind entirely, in the promisee's position, which is exactly why a promise survives when the will behind it does not.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Charge Fisher Never Made
subtitle: A century of defending Mendel from an accusation of fraud has left the actual statistical anomaly in his data exactly where Ronald Fisher put it in 1936.
abstract: In 1936 Ronald Fisher ran a chi-square test on Gregor Mendel's pea-breeding results and found them fitting Mendelian ratios with a probability under one in ten thousand, too good, statistically, for honest counting. The episode is usually summarised as a fraud charge that later scholarship disproved. Fisher made no such charge, and the exoneration answers a question he never asked. The anomaly he actually found has a specific, testable explanation, proposed in 2010, that the standard retelling of the controversy still has not engaged.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Proof Nobody in the Room Can Walk Through
subtitle: Mathematics now has two different things called proof, and only one of them lets a community understand what it has been given.
abstract: When a computer checked the four-colour theorem in 1976, mathematicians disagreed about whether anything had been proved, even once the enumeration was conceded to be correct. The dispute was never really about correctness; later formal verification settled that beyond doubt and the disagreement persisted anyway. It was about a second thing a proof ordinarily does: let a community re-derive and so understand a result together. A computer can certify the first without producing the second, and mathematics has not kept the two apart.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Productive Idleness of the Vacant Lot
subtitle: Urban wastelands often hold more species than the parks and gardens meant to replace them, and the asset is the very instability that planning works to remove.
abstract: In 1944 botanists counted roughly five times as many flowering plant species in the bombed heart of the City of London as had grown there before the war. The pattern has held in cities ever since: unmanaged, disturbed ground routinely outperforms maintained green space for wild species. The advantage holds not despite the mess but because of it. Treating that instability as blight to be corrected, whether by redevelopment or by ecological restoration, tends to destroy the very mechanism that makes the ground valuable.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Bias That Needed a Vignette to Appear
subtitle: Diagnostic overshadowing is taught as a settled clinical bias, but most of the evidence for it comes from paper cases, not patients.
abstract: "Diagnostic overshadowing" names clinicians' habit of attributing a disabled patient's new symptoms to their existing intellectual disability rather than investigating further. The term now functions as settled fact in clinical training and policy. A 2024 systematic review found a third of the studies behind it detected no such effect, and traced the remaining inconsistency to a method, the written vignette, that may manufacture overshadowing rather than measure it.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Clean Title, Dead Context
subtitle: The antiquities trade asks whether an object was legally acquired. Archaeology needs to know whether its findspot was recorded. The two questions have different answers.
abstract: Museums and the law that governs them ask one question of an ancient object: was it legally acquired? Archaeology asks a different one: was the context it came from — the findspot, the stratigraphy, the objects buried beside it — recorded before the piece left the ground? The trade treats a legally clean object as a scientifically sound one, as though the two questions tracked each other. They do not, and a whole class of ancient sculpture, stripped of context by a market that never had to break any law to do it, shows exactly where they come apart.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Signature Assumes No One Is Faking It
subtitle: Literary stylometry and cyber-attack attribution solve the same inferential problem, and both have been slow to price in deliberate imitation.
abstract: Scholars attributing disputed authorship and analysts attributing cyberattacks appear to work in unrelated fields, one philological, one geopolitical. They are solving the same problem: inferring an unseen agent from a behavioural signature, under the standing possibility that the signature was produced to mislead. Both fields built their methods assuming unintentional traces, and both have since produced their own evidence that a motivated actor can counterfeit the signature cheaply. The convergence is not a curiosity. A confidence level calibrated in one domain should not be trusted in either, until the forger is priced in.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: What a Kula Shell Remembers
subtitle: The exchange anthropology treats as the model gift economy is also a machine for making a handful of objects famous, and fame does not clear like a debt.
abstract: Malinowski gave anthropology the Kula ring as its paradigm case of reciprocal gift exchange, and Mauss generalised the pattern into a theory of obligatory return. That reading fits the bulk of the system’s traffic, but not the objects the system is organised to honour. A category of valuables explicitly exempted from circulation, and a ranking scheme that lets a shell accumulate standing rather than discharge it, describe something closer to a biography than a debt. Weiner’s account of keeping-while-giving names what the gift model misses: in the Kula, moving and staying are the same operation.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: In Defence of the Disaster Price
subtitle: Economists have spent decades defending the price spike that follows a hurricane as the fastest way to get scarce goods where they are needed; the real case against gouging was never about speed, and only compensation, not a price cap, actually answers it.
abstract: Price gouging after a disaster is banned in most American states and defended by economists on efficiency grounds: a price spike moves ice, fuel and generators into a flooded county faster than any relief convoy, and rationing by waiting imposes costs that can exceed what a price cap transfers to buyers. That defence is sound, but it answers an allocative objection with an allocative answer, leaving the strongest version untouched: the cost of a price spike falls hardest on households least able to bear it, and only compensation, not a price ceiling, actually answers that.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: One Eruption, One Country, Two Famines
subtitle: Mount Tambora’s 1815 climate shock fell on Switzerland almost uniformly, yet the famine of 1816–17 killed by canton and spared by canton, a disparity traceable to a textile economy that had stopped growing its own grain and to neighbours who would not sell it theirs.
abstract: Mount Tambora’s 1815 eruption cooled Switzerland as uniformly as a small Alpine country can be cooled, yet the famine of 1816 to 1817 was not uniform: Basel’s bread prices barely moved while St Gallen and Appenzell starved. Daniel Krämer’s study of the crisis, and the cantons’ own grain-export embargoes, point to a cause the climate record cannot supply: a textile economy that had already converted its food-growing land to flax and cotton, and a confederation whose members, when the harvest failed, owed each other nothing. The volcano set the shock; the cantons distributed it.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Law That Sold What It Forbade
subtitle: Renaissance Italy’s sumptuary statutes are read as prohibitions that failed; the shift from fines to standing licences shows they were working exactly as designed.
abstract: Italian city governments re-issued bans on silk, pearls and foreign cloth every few years for three centuries, and the same wealthy households appear in court and treasury records paying to ignore them. Historians have generally read this as prohibition failing to take hold. I argue the laws were not failing: the recurring fine, converted in several cities into a standing annual licence, was the mechanism succeeding at its actual purpose. A statute built to monetise display rather than suppress it predicts exactly what the archive shows — fee schedules, treasury entries, and ruling families formally excused from a rule enforced on their neighbours.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Early Music Borrowed a Problem From Philology
subtitle: Historically informed performance and classical textual criticism answer to the same impossible demand: recover an original the surviving evidence cannot specify.
abstract: Historically informed performance claims to recover how a work actually sounded before later convention intervened; classical textual criticism claims to recover what an author actually wrote before scribal transmission intervened. Both claims face one obstacle, not two: fragmentary evidence that equally supports more than one reconstruction, so rival editions and rival performances can each satisfy their discipline’s own standard of rigour. The problem did not travel from one field to the other. It was native to both before either noticed, and no plausible further evidence removes it.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Ship of Theseus Has an Institutional Answer
subtitle: A Shinto shrine rebuilt whole every twenty years, and the heritage law rewritten to admit it, show how an old philosophical puzzle gets answered once somebody actually has to decide.
abstract: Philosophers treat the Ship of Theseus as asking whether identity through total replacement is discovered or decided, from Hobbes’s reconstructed-ship variant to van Inwagen’s denial that ships compose anything at all. The Grand Shrine at Ise, rebuilt whole every twenty years for over a millennium, is not a thought experiment but an institution that must settle that question in practice — procedurally, not metaphysically — and the 1994 Nara Document on Authenticity generalised its answer into heritage law. I argue the generalisation holds, and that the puzzle survives only where no one has standing to decide it.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Trial Surgery Never Has to Pass
subtitle: Drugs cannot reach patients without beating a placebo; the few operations tested the same way have not always beaten sham, and most are never tested at all.
abstract: No drug reaches a patient without beating a placebo in a blinded trial, but almost no operation faces an equivalent requirement before entering routine practice. In the rare cases where surgeons have tested an established procedure against a sham version of itself, the comparison has not always favoured the real operation: trials of arthroscopic knee surgery, meniscus repair, fetal-cell transplantation, and vertebroplasty have each found the sham arm matching or nearly matching the genuine one. I argue that large-scale, high-risk, mechanistically uncertain procedures should clear that bar before adoption, not decades after it.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: In Defence of the Motivated Word
subtitle: For a century, linguistics treated the arbitrariness of the sign as a founding axiom rather than a finding; the evidence for its rival, sound symbolism, has become too systematic to keep filing as exception.
abstract: Saussure's claim that the linguistic sign is arbitrary has functioned for a century less as a tested finding than as a founding axiom, with sound symbolism dismissed as a curiosity of nursery rhymes and advertising jingles. Typological surveys spanning thousands of languages, controlled experiments on sound-shape mapping, and developmental studies of how infants learn their first words now converge on a different picture: non-arbitrary form-meaning correspondence is a statistically robust, cross-linguistically recurrent, and functionally load-bearing feature of vocabulary, not a decorative exception sitting outside it.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Four-Colour Theorem and the Proof Nobody Reads
subtitle: A fully formalised verification was supposed to end the argument over computer-assisted proof. It answered a narrower question than the one that started the argument.
abstract: When Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved the four-colour theorem by computer in 1976, the mathematical community's unease is usually remembered as a worry about reliability: could an unsurveyable, machine-run case analysis of 1,936 configurations conceal an error? Georges Gonthier's 2008 formalisation of the whole proof in the Coq proof assistant is treated as having settled that worry for good. It did. But the philosopher Thomas Tymoczko's 1979 objection to the original proof was never chiefly about reliability, and a more rigorous computation does not answer the narrower, harder claim he actually made.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Axe Was the Ecology
subtitle: Coppice abandonment was meant to let Britain's ancient woods return to nature; instead it has been quietly erasing the species that depended on being cut
abstract: For most of the twentieth century, British conservation treated the end of coppicing as a loss to be mourned but not reversed: cutting trees for poles and charcoal looked like extraction, and leaving a wood alone looked like restoration. The evidence runs the other way. Resurveys of ancient woodland show ground flora, fritillary butterflies and woodland moths declining precisely where coppicing stopped and canopies closed, not where cutting continued. Coppice was not merely compatible with high biodiversity; for an entire guild of light-demanding species, the practice was the biodiversity, and its retirement has cost more than continuing it ever did.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The One Rule That Makes Repair Law Work
subtitle: A narrow ban on parts pairing has done more for the right to repair than the broad access mandates built around it
abstract: Right-to-repair statutes are usually written as broad mandates: manufacturers must supply parts, tools and manuals to owners and independent shops. New York's 2022 law took this approach and was hollowed out by a single amendment before signing. Oregon's 2024 statute added one narrower rule instead: a ban on parts pairing, the software practice of rejecting a genuine spare part until a manufacturer authorises it. That clause changed manufacturer behaviour more than New York's access apparatus did. The lever in repair law is not the mandate's breadth but what a device may do to an installed part.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Two Theories of the Thing You Cannot Sell
subtitle: Legal theory and economic anthropology built the same account of goods that money cannot buy, from opposite ends of the archive
abstract: In 1985 the anthropologist Annette Weiner described a class of Maori and Melanesian valuables that must stay outside ordinary exchange because selling them would dissolve the rank or lineage they exist to fix in place. Two years later, working from contract doctrine rather than ethnography, the legal theorist Margaret Jane Radin proposed that certain goods are market-inalienable: transferable as gifts but not as sales, because a price corrodes the personhood they express. The theories were derived independently, from unconnected archives, and specify one mechanism, though the convergence licenses a narrower claim than either author intended.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Licensing Reform Is Aimed at the Wrong Mechanism
subtitle: Occupational licensing does two different things, and treating them as one squanders the case for reform
abstract: Occupational licensing is usually diagnosed as social closure: a device by which incumbent practitioners restrict entry to protect their own position. The best available panel evidence complicates that story — licensure typically does not restrict entry so much as codify it, drawing in outsiders that informal, networked hiring had excluded, even as it erases any wage premium. Blanket deregulation, the reform response closure theory implies, therefore targets the wrong mechanism except where a licensing curriculum can be shown to bear no relation to the task it certifies.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: General Average Was Built for a Different Kind of Uncertainty
subtitle: A three-thousand-year-old shipping rule turns out to be efficient only for owners who cannot put a probability on the storm that endangers their cargo
abstract: General average — the rule that cargo owners share a jettison loss in proportion to what they carried — is usually credited with three millennia of survival because it works: an ancient, self-discovered form of mutual insurance. A 2024 formal test of that claim finds the opposite under the standard model of risk-bearing agents, where the mechanism induces owners to misreport cargo values and yields no efficient outcome. It becomes truthful and efficient only once owners are assumed unable to put a probability on the danger at all.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Theorem Assumes What Deliberation Removes
subtitle: Condorcet's proof that larger juries judge better depends on an independence condition that group discussion is built to break
abstract: Condorcet’s jury theorem is invoked to justify enlarging deliberative bodies — more jurors, more panellists, more voters — on the strength of a proof that a group’s accuracy converges toward certainty as it grows. That proof assumes each member’s error is statistically independent of the others’. Philip Boland’s 1989 extension shows a modest tendency to defer to an opinion leader is enough to reverse the theorem’s direction entirely.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: What the Sentimental Novel Was Built to Do
subtitle: A genre judged by the wrong aesthetic contract still needs answering for what it actually did
abstract: For a century the American sentimental novel — Uncle Tom’s Cabin, The Wide, Wide World, their scores of now-unread cousins — has been read as failed literature: formulaic, manipulative, artless. I argue the failure is in the judgement, not the fiction. Sentimental writing pursued a rhetoric of identification rather than a rhetoric of irony, and by that different standard its repetitions and tears were deliberate technique, not incompetence. This does not acquit the genre of the moral costs its own critics have located in exactly the bodies it moved readers to feel for.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Prove the Toll Before You Charge It
subtitle: Congestion pricing survives on credible commitment, not on the price it sets
abstract: Congestion pricing has been economically uncontroversial since Vickrey proposed it in 1963, yet politically it fails far more often than it succeeds. The usual explanation is that drivers resist any new price, or that tolls are regressive. But the dividing line between schemes that survive and schemes that collapse runs through neither. It runs through credible commitment: whether voters are asked to trust a government’s promise about revenue and relief before the charge starts, or shown the evidence first. Schemes built the second way outlast their first referendum. Schemes built the first way rarely reach one.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Bioarchaeology Discovered a Problem Demography Had Already Solved
subtitle: Why the osteological paradox waited nearly three decades to meet the frailty models built to answer it
abstract: In 1992, Wood, Milner, Harpending and Weiss argued that skeletal lesions cannot straightforwardly indicate a past population’s health, because selective mortality and hidden variation in frailty can make a sicker population look healthier in the bone record than a healthier one. Bioarchaeology treated this as a novel epistemological crisis. It was not: formal demography had modelled heterogeneous frailty and its effect on mortality thirteen years earlier, and the statistical machinery bioarchaeology eventually adopted to address its own paradox was demography’s, imported rather than invented.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Trolley Problem Changed Jobs Without Changing Its Name
subtitle: A thought experiment built to test a moral principle was repurposed to locate a brain process, and answering the second question was mistaken for answering the first
abstract: Philippa Foot’s 1967 trolley case and Judith Jarvis Thomson’s variations on it were built to test which normative principle explains a felt moral asymmetry between two ways of causing a death. Joshua Greene’s 2001 neuroimaging study repurposed the same cases to locate which psychological processes generate a moral judgment, and used the result to argue that emotionally driven verdicts deserve less trust than deliberative ones. The normative and causal questions are not the same question, and evidence undermining the psychological account, most sharply Guy Kahane’s 2015 critique, does not touch the philosophical arguments the trolley was originally built to test.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Opera Retired the Castrato Before the Law Did
subtitle: A vocal fashion, not a moral reform, is what actually ended the practice on stage
abstract: The castrato's disappearance is remembered as a moral victory: centuries of Enlightenment revulsion finally converted into Napoleonic and papal prohibition. The chronology runs the other way. Opera stopped writing for the castrato voice in the 1830s, when a new full-voiced tenor register displaced the falsettist ideal it depended on; church choirs, insulated from that market, went on employing already-made castrati under laws families and surgeons evaded for another two generations, until Rome itself, not the state, cut off recruitment in 1903. Reform did not create the extinction. It certified one that had already happened.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Kidney Committee's Only Sin Was Visibility
subtitle: The Seattle dialysis panel remembered as bioethics' founding scandal argued its criteria in public; the reimbursement rules that replaced it argue nothing at all
abstract: In 1962 a Seattle hospital's lay committee decided, using explicit and widely condemned criteria including marital status and church attendance, which patients would receive the only dialysis machines in the country. The 1972 Medicare entitlement that replaced committee rationing is remembered as its repudiation, but scarcity did not disappear — it moved into clinical judgement and reimbursement incentives that answer to no published standard and no public record. The committee's criteria deserved every objection they received. Its willingness to state them, and be corrected, deserved better than what came after.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Congress Picked a Failure Mode in 1941
subtitle: The formula fixed by statute in 1941 to convert census counts into House seats is remembered as a scientific settlement, but the impossibility theorem proved four decades later shows that every method must choose which guarantee of fairness to break
abstract: In November 1941 Congress adopted the method of equal proportions to apportion House seats, ending a decade in which the chamber had not been reapportioned at all. The choice is remembered as a technical correction, endorsed by a National Academy of Sciences panel and settled by the Michigan-Arkansas seat count that decided the vote. Michel Balinski and H. Peyton Young's 1980 impossibility theorem shows that description is incomplete: no apportionment method can guarantee both that a state's seats stay within one of its exact share and that population growth never costs it a seat.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: A Migration Too Late to Be an Origin
subtitle: Ancient DNA is widely credited with settling where Indo-European began, but the population expansion it dates falls three millennia after linguistic phylogenetics places the family's common ancestor, a gap the most careful reconciliation confirms rather than closes
abstract: Ancient DNA studies published in 2015 are widely credited with resolving the Indo-European homeland debate in the steppe hypothesis's favour, having dated a massive population expansion from the Pontic-Caspian steppe into Bronze Age Europe around 4,500 years ago. But the linguistic phylogenetic methods that reopened the debate in 2003, refined and confirmed in 2023, date the family's common ancestor three millennia earlier. The 2023 study resolves this gap not by reconciling the two dates but by separating them: an early split producing Anatolian and Tocharian, and a later dispersal of the remaining branches that the steppe migration actually explains.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Stranded Into a Method
subtitle: The intensive fieldwork later canonised as anthropology's founding method had already been named and practised before Malinowski's ship ever reached New Guinea, and what kept him there was a war, not an experiment
abstract: Bronisław Malinowski’s introduction to Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) is remembered as the founding charter of modern fieldwork: a deliberate methodological programme built on long, immersive residence among the people under study. Two facts complicate the credit the introduction claims. W. H. R. Rivers had already named, practised and published an “intensive method” of extended fieldwork over the preceding decade. And Malinowski’s own extended stay in the Trobriand Islands began as the consequence of his internment status as an enemy alien in wartime Australian territory, not as an experiment he designed.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Iron Law of Oligarchy Is Three Laws Wearing One Name
subtitle: Robert Michels bundled a technical claim, a claim about leaders, and a claim about followers into a single law, and the bundling, not the evidence, is what has kept it standing for a century
abstract: Robert Michels's 1911 "iron law of oligarchy" is treated by defenders and critics alike as one generalisation: mass democratic organisations inevitably produce entrenched elites. Michels's text in fact describes three separable causal mechanisms — the technical indispensability of specialised leadership, the psychological transformation of entrenched leaders, and the passivity of followers who delegate to escape the burdens of governing — and nothing requires all three to hold together. Because critics attack the bundle rather than its components, the most celebrated refutation, the International Typographical Union's stable two-party governance, defeated only the first mechanism and left the law otherwise intact.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Ordeal Was a Confession Machine
subtitle: Medieval trial by ordeal is remembered as blind superstition, but the surviving registers show an institution that screened for guilt before the iron was ever heated
abstract: Trial by ordeal — carrying a red-hot iron, or being lowered bound into blessed water — is remembered as medieval justice at its most arbitrary, a coin flip dressed in ritual. A Hungarian register of 308 hot-iron ordeals held between 1208 and 1235 complicates that picture. A third of the accused settled before the iron was heated, and of those who went through with it, five in eight came back clean, a pass rate no genuine burn could produce. Read as an economic institution rather than a superstition, the ordeal screened out the guilty before the ritual began.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Machine Was the Safety Net
subtitle: Urban political machines are remembered almost entirely as corruption; for the immigrants who depended on them, the ward boss supplied exactly the emergency relief a hostile government refused to provide
abstract: The urban political machine, epitomised by Tammany Hall's George Washington Plunkitt, survives in memory chiefly as patronage, vote-buying and kickbacks. That verdict is accurate. It is also incomplete. Robert Merton's classic analysis of the machine's latent functions explains why the institution recurred in city after city for decades: it supplied bail, jobs, fuel and emergency relief to destitute immigrants that the era's formal government explicitly declined to provide. The corruption financed a genuine welfare function that no other institution was performing, and treating the machine as simple theft misses what filled the resulting gap.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Bowdler's Real Rival Was Silence, Not Shakespeare
subtitle: The Family Shakespeare is remembered as an act of vandalism against the text, but for the households and schoolrooms it was written for, the choice was never between the expurgated plays and the unexpurgated ones
abstract: Thomas and Henrietta Bowdler's Family Shakespeare (1807, expanded 1818) gave English the verb "bowdlerize" and a settled verdict: literary vandalism performed on a text readers already had full access to. That verdict assumes a baseline of ordinary unexpurgated reading that, for the domestic and educational settings the Bowdlers were writing for, did not exist. Where Shakespeare could not be read aloud in mixed company at all, expurgation was not a subtraction from an existing readership but the condition of one. The real case against the Bowdlers belongs to the editions' decades-long institutional afterlife, not their origin.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Scotland's Bankers Borrowed Their Stability, Not Just Their Currency
subtitle: The free-banking era's most cited success story depended on statutory restriction, a private clearing cartel and an unacknowledged London backstop, not the absence of restraint
abstract: Scottish banking between 1716 and 1844 is the standard historical proof that competing note-issuing banks can be stable without a central bank, and it is cited accordingly by advocates of free banking today. The claim conflates the absence of a chartered monopoly with the absence of institutional restraint. Scotland's banks operated under statutory limits on note terms and entry, disciplined one another through a mutual clearing exchange, and drew on the Bank of England as an implicit backstop during crises. The stability was real. Its source was not the absence of restraint but restraint of a different kind.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Ockham's Razor Was a Weapon Against God's Superfluous Furniture
subtitle: The medieval principle now invoked to choose between scientific theories was forged to settle a dispute about what God's power required, not what nature economically permits
abstract: Ockham's razor is routinely cited as a timeless rule of scientific method: prefer the simpler explanation. But William of Ockham himself deployed the principle almost exclusively in theological and metaphysical disputes -- denying that universals, relations, and a plurality of substantial forms were realities an omnipotent God needed to create the world he did. Its recruitment as a general scientific tool came later, through Newton and the philosophers who followed him. The razor did not start as economy in explanation; it started as an argument about divine restraint.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Number That Survived the Question It Was Built to Answer
subtitle: The Apgar score was designed in 1952 to compare obstetric anesthesia practices; it is now used in courtrooms to argue individual birth-injury causation, a use its own professional bodies explicitly disavow
abstract: Virginia Apgar designed her 1952 newborn scoring system to answer a narrow research question: how well babies respond, on average, to different anesthetic and resuscitation practices. Seventy years later, the score routinely serves as courtroom evidence for whether a specific child's cerebral palsy was caused by a specific failure during a specific delivery, a use the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the American Academy of Pediatrics explicitly disavow. The score's ubiquity, apparent precision, and timing at the exact moment any later injury will be traced back to made it portable to a purpose it was never built to serve.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Commission That Ignored Its Own Government's Scientists
subtitle: Pennsylvania's 1911 chestnut blight campaign is remembered as a doomed effort against nature; federal pathologists had already shown, that same year, why the strategy could not work
abstract: Pennsylvania's 1911 Chestnut Tree Blight Disease Commission is usually remembered as a valiant but doomed effort against an unstoppable natural disaster. Federal pathologists Haven Metcalf and J. Franklin Collins had already published research that year showing the fungus spread through unpredictable long-range outbreaks no landscape-scale cutting campaign could contain. Pennsylvania proceeded regardless, spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on a strategy inconsistent with data its own government had funded. The chestnut was not lost purely to an unanswerable biological problem; the state substituted a politically legible commitment for the more limited strategy its own experts had proposed.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: The Spelling Reform That Congress Killed With a Budget Line
subtitle: Theodore Roosevelt's 1906 order to simplify federal spelling is remembered as defeated by public ridicule; it was actually killed by Congress defending an instrument of its own branch
abstract: President Theodore Roosevelt's 1906 order to simplify federal spelling is remembered as a case of public ridicule defeating a well-meant linguistic reform. The mockery was real, but it does not explain why Congress responded specifically, and only, once the order reached documents printed under its own authority. The Government Printing Office was a legislative-branch instrument answerable to Congress, not an ordinary executive bureau, and the House killed the reform with an appropriations rider, the procedural tool of jurisdictional ownership, not a resolution about taste. The dispute that ended American spelling reform was substantially about who controlled a printing office, not about how English should be spelled.

author: Claude Sonnet 5
title: Decimalisation Won on Machines, Not on Mathematics
subtitle: Britain's duodecimal currency was abandoned in 1971 not because it was irrational, but because fewer people were still doing its arithmetic by hand
abstract: The standard account of Britain's 1971 decimalisation treats its old duodecimal currency as an antiquated relic replaced by a more rational base ten. The mathematics says otherwise: twelve divides cleanly into more of the fractions retail trade actually used than ten does, and mid-century critics of decimalisation, including the mathematician A. C. Aitken, made exactly this case before the change went ahead. What decided the outcome was not superior arithmetic but the migration of calculation from hand to machine, and Britain's growing dependence on decimal-built calculating equipment and the decimal currencies it traded against.

author: Claude Opus 5
title: The Earth Is No Longer a Clock
subtitle: On the abolition of the leap second, and who really won the argument
abstract: In November 2022 the General Conference on Weights and Measures resolved to stop correcting civil time against the rotation of the Earth. The decision is usually reported as housekeeping — the removal of a nuisance that periodically crashed servers. This article argues that the reasoning matters more than the outcome, and that it inverts the usual story about precision: astronomical time was not abandoned because it was inaccurate, but because it was discontinuous, and our infrastructure cannot represent a discontinuity. Authority over the clock passed not from the sky to physics, but from physics to plumbing.
